Where’s the Best Breakfast in New Orleans?

  • Show All Code
  • Hide All Code
  • View Source

7 million Yelp reviews, three ways to divide a city, and a rating that adjusts for easy and tough reviewers

If you only have one morning in New Orleans, head just outside downtown. Bywater & St. Roch (ZIP 70117) is the best area overall, Mid-City (70119) has the most top-10 spots, and the top-ranked spot is Swiss Confectionery. Downtown has the most choice, but not the best choice.

Best area
Bywater& St. Roch, ZIP 70117
Most top-10 spots
Mid-City4 of the top 10, ZIP 70119
Number 1 spot
Swiss ConfectioneryOrleans Ave, Mid-City
Restaurants studied
575with 159,552 reviews

1 The question

New Orleans is famous for its breakfasts: beignets, brunch and chicory coffee. But with one morning to spare, where should you go?

Where can someone find the best breakfast and coffee in New Orleans, and which area of the city is best for finding it?

A plain star average has two problems. Some restaurants have only a handful of reviews, and some reviewers give everything five stars while others almost never do. So in this project, “best” means:

  1. Rated well by reviewers who are hard to impress. Each review is compared with that reviewer’s own usual rating (the adjusted score).
  2. Enough evidence. A restaurant needs at least 10 reviews from active reviewers to be ranked.
  3. For areas: lots of good options, and restaurants that are rated above reviewers’ usual more often than not.

2 The data, and how the huge files were handled

The project uses two files from the Yelp Open Dataset: the business file (113 MB, 150,346 businesses) and the review file (5.1 GB, 6,990,280 reviews, from 2005 to January 2022).

The review file is bigger than a laptop’s memory can comfortably hold. So instead of opening it all at once, the code reads it 100,000 reviews at a time, keeps only the reviews of New Orleans restaurants, and throws the rest away before reading the next batch.

  • Streaming import. Both files are read with jsonlite::stream_in() and a handler function. Each batch is cut down to the needed columns before the next is read. Scanning all 7 million reviews took about 6 minutes.
  • Only what’s needed. Only the business and review files are pulled out of the Yelp archive.
  • Small, compressed outputs. Results are saved as xz-compressed .rds files. Review text is stored separately: the review table without text is 15 MB, the text alone 71 MB.
  • Raw files stay local. The raw JSON files are several gigabytes, more than GitHub allows, so they are listed in .gitignore and can be deleted once the .rds files are saved.
Show the code: R/import.R 
# =============================================================================
# R/import.R
# Yelp Open Dataset -> New Orleans restaurants + their reviews (compressed RDS)
#
# Run from the project root (the folder that contains README.md):
#   Rscript R/import.R
# or open the project in RStudio and source("R/import.R").
#
# Input  (put ONE of these in data/raw/):
#   - Yelp-JSON.zip                        (the file Yelp gives you), or
#   - yelp_dataset.tar                     (what is inside the zip), or
#   - yelp_academic_dataset_business.json  and
#     yelp_academic_dataset_review.json    (already extracted)
#
# Output (data/new_orleans/):
#   - business_new_orleans.rds      New Orleans restaurants (one row per business)
#   - reviews_new_orleans.rds       every review of those restaurants, no text
#   - review_text_new_orleans.rds   review_id + text (kept separate: large file)
#   - import_log.txt                row counts, timings, file sizes
#
# Design notes (for the "large-data management" section of the report):
#   * Both JSON files are read with jsonlite::stream_in() and a handler, so only
#     one page of records is in memory at a time. Each page is reduced to the
#     needed columns (and, for reviews, to New Orleans restaurants) before the
#     next page is read. The ~5 GB review file never has to fit in RAM.
#   * Only the two needed JSON files are pulled out of the tar archive.
#   * Outputs are saved with xz compression.
# =============================================================================

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(jsonlite)
  library(dplyr)
  library(stringr)
})

# ---- Settings ---------------------------------------------------------------

raw_dir <- "data/raw"
out_dir <- "data/new_orleans"

# Set to TRUE to delete the raw JSON / tar / zip files after the RDS files have
# been written and successfully read back. Leave FALSE until you are sure.
delete_raw_files <- FALSE

# Records read per page. Lower it (e.g. 25000) if your computer runs out of memory.
page_size <- 1e5

business_file <- file.path(raw_dir, "yelp_academic_dataset_business.json")
review_file   <- file.path(raw_dir, "yelp_academic_dataset_review.json")

dir.create(raw_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
dir.create(out_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

log_lines <- character()
log_msg <- function(...) {
  line <- paste0(format(Sys.time(), "%H:%M:%S"), "  ", paste0(...))
  message(line)
  log_lines <<- c(log_lines, line)
}
fmt <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)
mb <- function(path) sprintf("%.1f MB", file.size(path) / 1024^2)

# ---- Step 1: unzip / untar (only if the JSON files are not there yet) -------

needed_json <- basename(c(business_file, review_file))

if (!all(file.exists(c(business_file, review_file)))) {

  tar_file <- list.files(raw_dir, pattern = "\\.tar$", full.names = TRUE,
                         recursive = TRUE)[1]

  if (is.na(tar_file)) {
    zip_file <- list.files(raw_dir, pattern = "\\.zip$", full.names = TRUE)[1]
    if (is.na(zip_file)) {
      stop("No Yelp files found in ", raw_dir, ". See README.md for download steps.")
    }
    log_msg("Unzipping ", basename(zip_file), " (", mb(zip_file), ")")
    zip_members <- unzip(zip_file, list = TRUE)$Name
    tar_member  <- grep("\\.tar$", zip_members, value = TRUE)[1]
    if (is.na(tar_member)) {
      # Some copies of the zip hold the JSON files directly
      json_members <- zip_members[basename(zip_members) %in% needed_json]
      unzip(zip_file, files = json_members, exdir = raw_dir, junkpaths = TRUE)
    } else {
      unzip(zip_file, files = tar_member, exdir = raw_dir, junkpaths = TRUE)
      tar_file <- file.path(raw_dir, basename(tar_member))
    }
  }

  if (!is.na(tar_file) && file.exists(tar_file)) {
    log_msg("Extracting business + review JSON from ", basename(tar_file),
            " (", mb(tar_file), ")")
    tar_members  <- untar(tar_file, list = TRUE)
    json_members <- tar_members[basename(tar_members) %in% needed_json]
    untar(tar_file, files = json_members, exdir = raw_dir)
    # Move to data/raw/ in case the tar stores them inside a sub-folder
    for (m in json_members) {
      from <- file.path(raw_dir, m)
      to   <- file.path(raw_dir, basename(m))
      if (normalizePath(from) != normalizePath(to, mustWork = FALSE)) file.rename(from, to)
    }
  }

  if (!all(file.exists(c(business_file, review_file)))) {
    stop("Could not find both JSON files after extraction. Check ", raw_dir, ".")
  }
}

log_msg("Business JSON: ", mb(business_file), " | Review JSON: ", mb(review_file))

# Helper: keep the listed columns from a page, adding any that are missing
keep_cols <- function(df, cols) {
  for (col in setdiff(cols, names(df))) df[[col]] <- NA
  df[, cols, drop = FALSE]
}

# ---- Step 2: import businesses (streamed) -----------------------------------

business_cols <- c("business_id", "name", "address", "city", "state",
                   "postal_code", "latitude", "longitude", "stars",
                   "review_count", "categories")

t0 <- Sys.time()
business_pages <- list()
business_total <- 0

stream_in(
  file(business_file),
  handler = function(df) {
    business_total <<- business_total + nrow(df)
    df <- keep_cols(df, business_cols)
    # Keep Louisiana only at this stage; New Orleans is decided below
    business_pages[[length(business_pages) + 1]] <<- df[df$state %in% "LA", ]
  },
  pagesize = page_size,
  verbose = FALSE
)

business_la <- bind_rows(business_pages)
rm(business_pages); invisible(gc())

log_msg("Businesses read: ", fmt(business_total),
        " | in Louisiana: ", fmt(nrow(business_la)),
        " | ", round(difftime(Sys.time(), t0, units = "secs")), " s")

# ---- Step 3: filter to New Orleans restaurants ------------------------------

# How is "New Orleans" spelled in the city field? (useful for the report)
city_spellings <- business_la |>
  filter(str_detect(str_to_lower(city), "new\\s*orleans")) |>
  count(city, sort = TRUE)
message("\nCity labels containing 'New Orleans':")
print(as.data.frame(city_spellings), row.names = FALSE)

new_orleans_restaurants <- business_la |>
  filter(
    state == "LA",
    str_to_lower(str_squish(city)) == "new orleans",
    !is.na(categories),
    str_detect(categories, regex("Restaurants", ignore_case = TRUE))
  ) |>
  mutate(
    city          = str_squish(city),
    postal_code   = na_if(postal_code, ""),
    categories    = str_squish(categories),
    business_name = str_squish(name)
  ) |>
  distinct(business_id, .keep_all = TRUE)

rm(business_la); invisible(gc())

log_msg("New Orleans restaurants: ",
        fmt(nrow(new_orleans_restaurants)))

print(
  new_orleans_restaurants |>
    summarise(
      number_of_restaurants = n(),
      missing_latitude   = sum(is.na(latitude)),
      missing_longitude  = sum(is.na(longitude)),
      missing_categories = sum(is.na(categories)),
      missing_postal     = sum(is.na(postal_code))
    )
)

# ---- Step 4: import reviews for those restaurants only (streamed) -----------

review_cols <- c("review_id", "business_id", "user_id", "stars", "date",
                 "text", "useful", "funny", "cool")
nola_ids <- new_orleans_restaurants$business_id

t0 <- Sys.time()
review_pages <- list()
review_total <- 0

stream_in(
  file(review_file),
  handler = function(df) {
    review_total <<- review_total + nrow(df)
    df <- df[df$business_id %in% nola_ids, , drop = FALSE]
    if (nrow(df) > 0) {
      review_pages[[length(review_pages) + 1]] <<- keep_cols(df, review_cols)
    }
    if (review_total %% 1e6 < page_size) {
      message("  ...", fmt(review_total), " reviews scanned")
    }
  },
  pagesize = page_size,
  verbose = FALSE
)

reviews_all_cols <- bind_rows(review_pages)
rm(review_pages); invisible(gc())

log_msg("Reviews scanned: ", fmt(review_total),
        " | kept for New Orleans restaurants: ",
        fmt(nrow(reviews_all_cols)),
        " | ", round(difftime(Sys.time(), t0, units = "mins"), 1), " min")

# Split the review text off: it is most of the file size and is not needed for
# the ratings analysis. review_id links the two tables if you need the text.
new_orleans_reviews <- reviews_all_cols |> select(-text)
new_orleans_review_text <- reviews_all_cols |> select(review_id, business_id, text)
rm(reviews_all_cols); invisible(gc())

# ---- Step 5: save as compressed RDS and verify ------------------------------

out_business <- file.path(out_dir, "business_new_orleans.rds")
out_reviews  <- file.path(out_dir, "reviews_new_orleans.rds")
out_text     <- file.path(out_dir, "review_text_new_orleans.rds")

saveRDS(new_orleans_restaurants, out_business, compress = "xz")
saveRDS(new_orleans_reviews,     out_reviews,  compress = "xz")
saveRDS(new_orleans_review_text, out_text,     compress = "xz")

check_business <- readRDS(out_business)
check_reviews  <- readRDS(out_reviews)
check_text     <- readRDS(out_text)
stopifnot(
  identical(dim(check_business), dim(new_orleans_restaurants)),
  identical(dim(check_reviews),  dim(new_orleans_reviews)),
  identical(dim(check_text),     dim(new_orleans_review_text))
)

log_msg("Saved ", basename(out_business), " (", mb(out_business), "), ",
        basename(out_reviews), " (", mb(out_reviews), "), ",
        basename(out_text), " (", mb(out_text), ")")

if (file.size(out_text) > 95 * 1024^2) {
  log_msg("NOTE: ", basename(out_text), " is over GitHub's 100 MB limit; ",
          "it is listed in .gitignore and stays on your computer.")
}

message("\nglimpse(business):"); glimpse(new_orleans_restaurants)
message("\nglimpse(reviews):");  glimpse(new_orleans_reviews)

# ---- Step 6: optionally delete the raw files --------------------------------

if (delete_raw_files) {
  raw_files <- list.files(raw_dir, pattern = "\\.(json|tar|zip)$",
                          full.names = TRUE, recursive = TRUE)
  freed <- sum(file.size(raw_files)) / 1024^3
  file.remove(raw_files)
  log_msg("Deleted ", length(raw_files), " raw files, freed ",
          sprintf("%.1f GB", freed))
}

writeLines(log_lines, file.path(out_dir, "import_log.txt"))
message("\nDone. Load the data later with:\n",
        "  new_orleans_restaurants <- readRDS(\"", out_business, "\")\n",
        "  new_orleans_reviews     <- readRDS(\"", out_reviews, "\")")

3 Choosing the restaurants

New Orleans restaurants. A business counts if state is LA, its city is “New Orleans”, and its categories include “Restaurants”. That gives 2,261 restaurants.

Breakfast & coffee. Four categories describe places you’d go for a morning meal or a coffee break: Breakfast & Brunch, Coffee & Tea, Cafes and Bakeries.

These four belong together because they often appear on the same restaurant:

Category pair Restaurants with both
Breakfast & Brunch + Coffee & Tea 85
Cafes + Coffee & Tea 75
Breakfast & Brunch + Cafes 65
Bakeries + Coffee & Tea 37
Bakeries + Breakfast & Brunch 32
Bakeries + Cafes 16

A restaurant is included if it has at least one of the four categories. That gives 575 restaurants spread over 24 ZIP code areas, far more than the required 10 restaurants in 7 areas. Their 159,552 reviews, from 97,950 different reviewers, were pulled out before any further analysis.

Show the code: R/clean.R 
# =============================================================================
# R/clean.R
# Step 3: select a related category group (breakfast & coffee)
# Step 4: join businesses to reviews for just that category group
#
# Run from the project root, after R/import.R:
#   Rscript R/clean.R
# =============================================================================

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(dplyr)
  library(stringr)
  library(tidyr)
})

business <- readRDS("data/new_orleans/business_new_orleans.rds")
reviews  <- readRDS("data/new_orleans/reviews_new_orleans.rds")

dir.create("data/new_orleans", showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

# ---- Step 3: category selection --------------------------------------------

# One row per business-category combination, cleaned up.
restaurant_categories <- business |>
  select(business_id, categories) |>
  separate_rows(categories, sep = ",") |>
  mutate(category = str_squish(categories)) |>
  select(business_id, category)

category_counts <- restaurant_categories |>
  count(category, sort = TRUE)

write.csv(category_counts, "data/new_orleans/category_counts.csv", row.names = FALSE)

# Theme: breakfast & coffee. These four categories are all places New Orleans
# residents/visitors go for a morning meal or a coffee break, so they support
# one focused question: "Where can someone find the best breakfast and coffee
# in New Orleans, and which area is best for finding it?"
selected_categories <- c("Breakfast & Brunch", "Coffee & Tea", "Cafes", "Bakeries")

# Co-occurrence among the selected categories (how often they overlap on the
# same business) -- evidence that they form one coherent group rather than
# four unrelated ones.
category_pairs <- restaurant_categories |>
  filter(category %in% selected_categories) |>
  inner_join(
    restaurant_categories |> filter(category %in% selected_categories),
    by = "business_id",
    relationship = "many-to-many"
  ) |>
  filter(category.x < category.y) |>
  count(category.x, category.y, sort = TRUE)

message("Category counts for the selected group:")
print(category_counts |> filter(category %in% selected_categories))
message("\nCo-occurrence between selected categories:")
print(category_pairs)

# Inclusion rule: a restaurant qualifies if it has AT LEAST ONE of the four
# selected categories.
selected_restaurant_ids <- restaurant_categories |>
  filter(category %in% selected_categories) |>
  distinct(business_id) |>
  pull(business_id)

selected_restaurants <- business |>
  filter(business_id %in% selected_restaurant_ids)

n_areas <- n_distinct(selected_restaurants$postal_code, na.rm = TRUE)

message(
  "\nQualifying restaurants: ", nrow(selected_restaurants),
  " across ", n_areas, " ZIP codes (requirement: >= 10 restaurants, >= 7 areas)"
)
stopifnot(nrow(selected_restaurants) >= 10, n_areas >= 7)

saveRDS(selected_restaurants, "data/new_orleans/selected_restaurants.rds")

# ---- Step 4: join reviews to the selected restaurants only -----------------

selected_reviews <- reviews |>
  semi_join(selected_restaurants, by = "business_id")

message(
  "\nReviews for selected (breakfast & coffee) restaurants: ",
  nrow(selected_reviews), " out of ", nrow(reviews), " total New Orleans reviews"
)

saveRDS(selected_reviews, "data/new_orleans/selected_reviews.rds")

message("\nSaved data/new_orleans/selected_restaurants.rds, selected_reviews.rds, category_counts.csv")

4 Checking the city boundary

Yelp’s city field is just text typed by the business. To check it, each restaurant’s latitude and longitude were matched to the official city boundary from the U.S. Census with a spatial join.

Yelp city Official place Restaurants
New Orleans New Orleans 564
New Orleans Elmwood 2
New Orleans Harahan 2
New Orleans Jefferson 2
New Orleans Metairie 2
New Orleans Terrytown 2
New Orleans Kenner 1

11 restaurants have a New Orleans mailing address but sit just outside the city limits, in Jefferson Parish. They are real nearby options, so they stay in.

Show the code: R/analysis.R 
# =============================================================================
# R/analysis.R
# Step 5: spatial join to an official city boundary (tigris::places)
# Step 6: compare two geographic systems (ZCTA vs. Census tract) and pick one
#
# Run from the project root, after R/clean.R:
#   Rscript R/analysis.R
# =============================================================================

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(dplyr)
  library(sf)
  library(tigris)
  library(ggplot2)
  library(viridis)
})

options(tigris_use_cache = TRUE)
dir.create("figures", showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

selected_restaurants <- readRDS("data/new_orleans/selected_restaurants.rds")

restaurant_points <- selected_restaurants |>
  filter(!is.na(longitude), !is.na(latitude)) |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326, remove = FALSE)

# ---- Step 5: spatial join to the official New Orleans place boundary -------

louisiana_places <- tigris::places(state = "LA", cb = TRUE, year = 2024, class = "sf") |>
  st_transform(4326)

restaurants_with_place <- restaurant_points |>
  st_join(
    louisiana_places |> select(GEOID, place_name = NAME),
    join = st_within,
    left = TRUE
  )

message("Yelp city label vs. official place boundary:")
city_vs_place <- restaurants_with_place |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  count(city, place_name, sort = TRUE)
print(as.data.frame(head(city_vs_place, 15)))

new_orleans_boundary <- louisiana_places |> filter(NAME == "New Orleans")
new_orleans_map_data <- restaurants_with_place |> filter(place_name == "New Orleans")

p_boundary <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = new_orleans_boundary, fill = "grey95", color = "grey35") +
  geom_sf(data = new_orleans_map_data, aes(color = stars), alpha = 0.7, size = 1.5) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(option = "C", limits = c(1, 5)) +
  labs(
    title = "Breakfast & Coffee Spots Within the New Orleans City Boundary",
    color = "Business\nstars"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

ggsave("figures/new_orleans_boundary_map.png", p_boundary, width = 7, height = 6, dpi = 150)

# ---- Step 6: compare two geographic systems ---------------------------------

# System 1: ZIP Code Tabulation Areas (ZCTA)
zctas_la <- tigris::zctas(state = "LA", cb = FALSE, year = 2010, class = "sf") |>
  select(area_id = ZCTA5CE10) |>
  st_transform(4326)

restaurants_by_zcta <- restaurant_points |>
  st_join(zctas_la, join = st_within, left = TRUE)

zcta_summary <- restaurants_by_zcta |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  group_by(area_id) |>
  summarise(
    number_of_restaurants = n(),
    average_business_stars = mean(stars, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(number_of_restaurants))

# System 2: Census tracts (Orleans Parish)
tracts_orleans <- tigris::tracts(state = "LA", county = "Orleans", cb = TRUE, year = 2024, class = "sf") |>
  select(area_id = TRACTCE) |>
  st_transform(4326)

restaurants_by_tract <- restaurant_points |>
  st_join(tracts_orleans, join = st_within, left = TRUE)

tract_summary <- restaurants_by_tract |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  group_by(area_id) |>
  summarise(
    number_of_restaurants = n(),
    average_business_stars = mean(stars, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(number_of_restaurants))

summarise_system <- function(df, label, n_areas_total) {
  matched <- df |> filter(!is.na(area_id))
  unmatched_n <- sum(is.na(df$area_id))
  tibble(
    geographic_system = label,
    number_of_areas = n_distinct(matched$area_id),
    restaurants_assigned = nrow(matched),
    unmatched_restaurants = unmatched_n,
    smallest_area_count = min(matched |> count(area_id) |> pull(n)),
    largest_area_count = max(matched |> count(area_id) |> pull(n))
  )
}

geographic_comparison <- bind_rows(
  summarise_system(st_drop_geometry(restaurants_by_zcta), "ZIP/ZCTA"),
  summarise_system(st_drop_geometry(restaurants_by_tract), "Census tract")
)

message("\nGeographic system comparison:")
print(as.data.frame(geographic_comparison))

write.csv(geographic_comparison, "data/new_orleans/geographic_comparison.csv", row.names = FALSE)
saveRDS(zcta_summary, "data/new_orleans/zcta_summary.rds")
saveRDS(tract_summary, "data/new_orleans/tract_summary.rds")

# Map of restaurant counts per ZCTA (the system this project selects -- see
# README for the justification).
zcta_map_data <- zctas_la |> left_join(zcta_summary, by = "area_id")

p_zcta <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = zcta_map_data, aes(fill = number_of_restaurants), color = "white", size = 0.1) +
  geom_sf(data = new_orleans_boundary, fill = NA, color = "black", linewidth = 0.6) +
  coord_sf(xlim = st_bbox(new_orleans_boundary)[c("xmin", "xmax")],
           ylim = st_bbox(new_orleans_boundary)[c("ymin", "ymax")]) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "C", na.value = "grey90") +
  labs(
    title = "Breakfast & Coffee Restaurants per ZIP Code (ZCTA)",
    fill = "Restaurant\ncount"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

ggsave("figures/zcta_restaurant_count_map.png", p_zcta, width = 7, height = 6, dpi = 150)

message("\nSaved figures/new_orleans_boundary_map.png, figures/zcta_restaurant_count_map.png")
message("Saved data/new_orleans/geographic_comparison.csv, zcta_summary.rds, tract_summary.rds")

5 Choosing a way to divide the city

To compare areas, the city has to be divided up somehow. Three systems were tested:

  • ZIP Code Tabulation Areas, the Census version of ZIP codes;
  • Neighborhood Statistical Areas, the City of New Orleans’ own planning neighbourhoods;
  • Census tracts, statistical areas built for population data.
System Areas with a restaurant Assigned Unmatched Smallest Largest Median per area Areas with < 5
ZIP codes 24 575 0 1 143 6.5 9 (38%)
Neighbourhoods 54 564 11 1 119 4 28 (52%)
Census tracts 103 564 11 1 117 2 75 (73%)

The smaller the areas, the fewer restaurants each one holds, and the more one restaurant can swing the average. Three out of four census tracts have fewer than 5 breakfast spots.

The choice: ZIP codes

enough restaurants per area · easy to understand · every restaurant matched

  • Enough restaurants to compare. ZIP codes pool enough restaurants for the averages to mean something.
  • Easy to understand. Anyone knows a ZIP code. Few people know their census tract number.
  • Nothing left out. Every restaurant was matched to a ZIP code, including the 11 just outside the city.

What ZIP codes hide. ZIP codes are postal areas, not neighbourhoods. 70130 alone covers the Warehouse District and part of the French Quarter, so a great café and a tourist trap share one average. The 9 ZIP codes with fewer than 5 breakfast spots are mapped but not ranked.

Show the code: R/neighborhoods.R 
# =============================================================================
# R/neighborhoods.R
# Step 6 (third system): Neighborhood Statistical Areas (NSAs), the City of
# New Orleans' own planning neighbourhoods. Also rebuilds the geographic
# comparison table with all three systems.
#
# Run from the project root, after R/analysis.R and R/boundaries.R:
#   Rscript R/neighborhoods.R
# =============================================================================

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(dplyr)
  library(sf)
})
sf_use_s2(FALSE)

selected_restaurants <- readRDS("data/new_orleans/selected_restaurants.rds")
restaurant_points <- selected_restaurants |>
  filter(!is.na(longitude), !is.na(latitude)) |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326, remove = FALSE)

nsa  <- st_read("data/boundaries/nsa_new_orleans.geojson", quiet = TRUE)
zcta <- st_read("data/boundaries/zcta_new_orleans.geojson", quiet = TRUE)

# Assign every restaurant to a ZIP code and a neighbourhood
restaurant_areas <- restaurant_points |>
  st_join(zcta, join = st_within, left = TRUE) |>
  rename(zip = area_id) |>
  st_join(nsa, join = st_within, left = TRUE) |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(business_id, zip, neighborhood)
saveRDS(restaurant_areas, "data/new_orleans/restaurant_areas.rds")

nsa_summary <- restaurant_points |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  left_join(restaurant_areas, by = "business_id") |>
  group_by(area_id = neighborhood) |>
  summarise(
    number_of_restaurants  = n(),
    average_business_stars = mean(stars, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(number_of_restaurants))
saveRDS(nsa_summary, "data/new_orleans/nsa_summary.rds")

# ---- Comparison table with all three systems --------------------------------

summarise_system <- function(summary, label) {
  matched <- summary |> filter(!is.na(area_id))
  tibble(
    geographic_system     = label,
    number_of_areas       = nrow(matched),
    restaurants_assigned  = sum(matched$number_of_restaurants),
    unmatched_restaurants = sum(summary$number_of_restaurants[is.na(summary$area_id)]),
    smallest_area_count   = min(matched$number_of_restaurants),
    largest_area_count    = max(matched$number_of_restaurants)
  )
}

geographic_comparison <- bind_rows(
  summarise_system(readRDS("data/new_orleans/zcta_summary.rds"),  "ZIP/ZCTA"),
  summarise_system(readRDS("data/new_orleans/tract_summary.rds"), "Census tract"),
  summarise_system(nsa_summary, "Neighborhood Statistical Area")
)
print(as.data.frame(geographic_comparison))
print(head(as.data.frame(nsa_summary), 12))
write.csv(geographic_comparison, "data/new_orleans/geographic_comparison.csv", row.names = FALSE)
message("Saved restaurant_areas.rds, nsa_summary.rds, geographic_comparison.csv")
Show the code: R/compare_systems.R 
# =============================================================================
# R/compare_systems.R
# Step 6 (continued): compare ZIP/ZCTA, census tracts and Neighborhood
# Statistical Areas on area size and average business rating, using the
# summaries saved by R/analysis.R and R/neighborhoods.R.
# Also draws the headline chart for the README.
#
# Run from the project root, after R/neighborhoods.R:
#   Rscript R/compare_systems.R
# =============================================================================

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(dplyr)
  library(ggplot2)
})
source("R/theme.R")

min_restaurants <- 5   # areas below this are mapped but not ranked

selected_restaurants <- readRDS("data/new_orleans/selected_restaurants.rds")
city_average <- mean(selected_restaurants$stars, na.rm = TRUE)

zcta_summary  <- readRDS("data/new_orleans/zcta_summary.rds")  |> mutate(system = "ZIP codes")
tract_summary <- readRDS("data/new_orleans/tract_summary.rds") |> mutate(system = "Census tracts")
nsa_summary   <- readRDS("data/new_orleans/nsa_summary.rds")   |> mutate(system = "Neighborhoods (NSAs)")

system_levels <- c("ZIP codes", "Neighborhoods (NSAs)", "Census tracts")
areas <- bind_rows(zcta_summary, tract_summary, nsa_summary) |>
  filter(!is.na(area_id)) |>
  mutate(system = factor(system, levels = system_levels))

# ---- Table: area size and rating by geographic system -----------------------

system_ratings <- areas |>
  group_by(system) |>
  summarise(
    number_of_areas              = n(),
    median_restaurants_per_area  = median(number_of_restaurants),
    areas_under_5                = sum(number_of_restaurants < min_restaurants),
    pct_areas_under_5            = round(100 * mean(number_of_restaurants < min_restaurants)),
    restaurants_in_areas_under_5 = sum(number_of_restaurants[number_of_restaurants < min_restaurants]),
    lowest_area_avg_stars        = round(min(average_business_stars[number_of_restaurants >= min_restaurants]), 2),
    highest_area_avg_stars       = round(max(average_business_stars[number_of_restaurants >= min_restaurants]), 2),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
print(as.data.frame(system_ratings))
write.csv(system_ratings, "data/new_orleans/system_ratings_comparison.csv", row.names = FALSE)

# ---- ZIP-level table (areas with enough restaurants to compare) -------------

# Main neighborhoods in each ZIP code, for readable labels
zip_neighborhoods <- c(
  "70112" = "CBD & Tulane-Gravier",      "70113" = "Central City",
  "70114" = "Algiers Point",             "70115" = "Uptown & Garden District",
  "70116" = "French Quarter & Marigny",  "70117" = "Bywater & St. Roch",
  "70118" = "Carrollton & Audubon",      "70119" = "Mid-City",
  "70122" = "Gentilly",                  "70124" = "Lakeview",
  "70125" = "Broadmoor & Freret",        "70126" = "New Orleans East",
  "70128" = "New Orleans East",          "70130" = "Warehouse District & upper Quarter",
  "70131" = "Algiers"
)

zcta_table <- zcta_summary |>
  filter(number_of_restaurants >= min_restaurants) |>
  transmute(zip = area_id,
            neighborhoods = unname(zip_neighborhoods[area_id]),
            restaurants = number_of_restaurants,
            average_business_stars = round(average_business_stars, 2)) |>
  arrange(desc(restaurants))
write.csv(zcta_table, "data/new_orleans/zcta_ratings.csv", row.names = FALSE)

# ---- Headline chart: average stars by ZIP vs. the city average --------------

hero <- zcta_table |>
  mutate(
    label    = paste0(zip, "  ", neighborhoods),
    label    = reorder(label, average_business_stars),
    better   = average_business_stars >= city_average,
    deep     = ifelse(better, theme_cols$above[["deep"]], theme_cols$below[["deep"]]),
    pastel   = ifelse(better, theme_cols$above[["fill"]], theme_cols$below[["fill"]]),
    value    = sprintf("%.2f", average_business_stars),
    count    = paste0(restaurants, " spots")
  )

p_hero <- ggplot(hero, aes(y = label)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = city_average, linetype = "22", color = theme_cols$ink, linewidth = 0.6) +
  annotate("text", x = city_average, y = Inf, vjust = -0.5, label = "city average",
           family = plot_family, fontface = "bold", color = theme_cols$ink, size = 3.8, hjust = 0.5) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = city_average, xend = average_business_stars, yend = label, color = pastel),
               linewidth = 3.2, lineend = "round") +
  geom_point(aes(x = average_business_stars, fill = deep), shape = 21, color = "white",
             size = 5, stroke = 1.2) +
  geom_text(aes(x = average_business_stars, label = value,
                hjust = ifelse(better, -0.55, 1.55)),
            family = plot_family, fontface = "bold", color = theme_cols$ink, size = 3.9) +
  geom_text(aes(x = 4.62, label = count), family = plot_family, color = theme_cols$muted,
            size = 3.5, hjust = 1) +
  scale_color_identity() +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(2.05, 4.62), breaks = seq(2.5, 4.5, 0.5)) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(
    title = "Most spots downtown, best ratings in Bywater",
    subtitle = "Average Yelp stars of breakfast & coffee restaurants, ZIP codes with at least 5 of them",
    x = "average business stars", y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_pastel() +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())

save_plot(p_hero, "figures/zip_ratings_chart.png", width = 10, height = 6.4)

# ---- Comparison plot: restaurants per area vs. average rating ---------------

system_colors <- c("ZIP codes" = theme_cols$zcta[["deep"]], "Census tracts" = theme_cols$tract[["deep"]],
                   "Neighborhoods (NSAs)" = theme_cols$nsa[["deep"]])

p_compare <- ggplot(areas, aes(number_of_restaurants, average_business_stars)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 0.8, xmax = min_restaurants - 0.5, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = theme_cols$band) +
  annotate("text", x = 2, y = 5.35, label = "too few to trust", family = plot_family,
           fontface = "bold", color = theme_cols$muted, size = 3.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = city_average, linetype = "22", color = theme_cols$ink, linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(aes(fill = system), shape = 21, color = "white", size = 3.4, stroke = 0.8, alpha = 0.9,

  ) +

save_plot(p_compare, "figures/geographic_system_comparison.png", width = 12, height = 5)

message("Saved figures/zip_ratings_chart.png, figures/geographic_system_comparison.png, ",
        "data/new_orleans/system_ratings_comparison.csv, zcta_ratings.csv")

6 Adjusting for reviewer habits

Some reviewers give almost every restaurant five stars; others rarely do. A 4-star review means more from a tough reviewer than from an easy one.

For each reviewer, work out their usual rating. Then score every review as stars given minus that reviewer’s usual. A reviewer who usually gives 3 stars and gives a place 4 adds +1. A reviewer who usually gives 5 and gives 4 adds −1. A restaurant’s adjusted score is the average of these.

Who counts as an active reviewer? A usual rating only means something if the reviewer has rated enough places. Reviewers with at least 5 breakfast & coffee reviews were kept:

Minimum reviews Reviewers kept Share of reviewers Reviews kept Share of reviews Restaurants ranked
3 11,531 11.8% 57,617 36.1% 448
5 3,416 3.5% 30,918 19.4% 394
10 784 0.8% 14,919 9.4% 325

Only 3.5% of reviewers qualify, but they wrote almost a fifth of all reviews. A higher threshold gives each reviewer a better baseline, but leaves fewer restaurants to rank.

Mean or median? The mean was used as each reviewer’s usual rating. Ratings are whole stars, so with a median baseline 49% of reviews get an adjusted score of exactly 0, throwing away most of the information. With the mean, only 5% do. The typical active reviewer averages 4.0 stars, but the range is wide: 2.9 at the 5th percentile, 4.8 at the 95th.

Ranks before and after adjustment are strongly related (rank correlation 0.83), but a few restaurants move hundreds of places:

Restaurant ZIP Stars (all reviewers) Stars (active reviewers) Rank before Rank after
First Cup Cafe 70125 3.44 4.47 331st 12th
Chris’ Cakes and Donuts 70128 3.00 3.82 374th 142nd
Rare Form 70116 3.85 4.27 251st 29th
Le Citron Bistro 70130 3.81 4.10 260th 38th
The Flying Pig Cafe 70115 4.13 3.30 161st 365th
Louise 70117 4.21 3.83 125th 320th
Wakin’ Bakin’ 70115 4.23 3.79 121st 307th
Streetcar Cafe 70130 4.39 4.19 74th 259th

The moves have two causes. Reviewer behaviour: First Cup Cafe’s active reviewers rate it a full star higher than casual reviewers do. Small samples: most of these restaurants have only 10 to 25 active-reviewer reviews, so a few reviews move them a long way.

Show the code: R/reviewers.R 
# =============================================================================
# R/reviewers.R
# Step 7: ratings from all reviewers vs. reviewer-adjusted scores
#
# Run from the project root, after R/clean.R:
#   Rscript R/reviewers.R
#
# Idea: some reviewers give almost everything 5 stars, others rarely do.
# For each reviewer we compute their usual (baseline) rating across the
# breakfast & coffee restaurants they reviewed, and subtract it from each of
# their ratings. A normalized score of +0.6 means "this reviewer rated this
# place 0.6 stars above what they usually give". It is NOT a new Yelp rating.
# =============================================================================

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(dplyr)
  library(tidyr)
  library(lubridate)
  library(ggplot2)
  library(ggrepel)
})
source("R/theme.R")

min_reviewer_reviews   <- 5    # a reviewer needs this many reviews to get a baseline
min_eligible_reviews   <- 10   # a restaurant needs this many eligible reviews to be ranked
thresholds_to_test     <- c(3, 5, 10)

selected_restaurants <- readRDS("data/new_orleans/selected_restaurants.rds")
category_reviews <- readRDS("data/new_orleans/selected_reviews.rds") |>
  mutate(review_date = ymd_hms(date), review_year = year(review_date))

# ---- All reviewers -----------------------------------------------------------

all_reviewer_summary <- category_reviews |>
  group_by(business_id) |>
  summarise(
    number_of_reviews_all_reviewers = n(),
    average_stars_all_reviewers     = mean(stars, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_stars_all_reviewers      = median(stars, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# ---- Reviewer activity and baselines -------------------------------------------

reviewer_baselines <- category_reviews |>
  group_by(user_id) |>
  summarise(
    reviewer_mean         = mean(stars, na.rm = TRUE),
    reviewer_median       = median(stars, na.rm = TRUE),
    reviewer_review_count = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

category_reviews_adjusted <- category_reviews |>
  left_join(reviewer_baselines, by = "user_id") |>
  mutate(
    normalized_mean_score   = stars - reviewer_mean,
    normalized_median_score = stars - reviewer_median
  )

# How many reviewers and reviews survive each activity threshold?
threshold_table <- tibble(min_reviews = thresholds_to_test) |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(
    reviewers_kept     = sum(reviewer_baselines$reviewer_review_count >= min_reviews),
    pct_of_reviewers   = round(100 * reviewers_kept / nrow(reviewer_baselines), 1),
    reviews_kept       = sum(category_reviews_adjusted$reviewer_review_count >= min_reviews),
    pct_of_reviews     = round(100 * reviews_kept / nrow(category_reviews_adjusted), 1),
    restaurants_ranked = category_reviews_adjusted |>
      filter(reviewer_review_count >= min_reviews) |>
      count(business_id) |>
      filter(n >= min_eligible_reviews) |>
      nrow()
  ) |>
  ungroup()

# Why the mean baseline: with whole-star ratings, the median baseline gives a
# normalized score of exactly 0 for a large share of reviews.
eligible_adjusted_reviews <- category_reviews_adjusted |>
  filter(reviewer_review_count >= min_reviewer_reviews)

baseline_check <- tibble(
  share_zero_with_median_baseline = round(mean(eligible_adjusted_reviews$normalized_median_score == 0), 3),
  share_zero_with_mean_baseline   = round(mean(abs(eligible_adjusted_reviews$normalized_mean_score) < 1e-9), 3),
  typical_reviewer_mean           = round(median(reviewer_baselines$reviewer_mean[reviewer_baselines$reviewer_review_count >= min_reviewer_reviews]), 2),
  reviewer_mean_5th_percentile    = round(quantile(reviewer_baselines$reviewer_mean[reviewer_baselines$reviewer_review_count >= min_reviewer_reviews], 0.05), 2),
  reviewer_mean_95th_percentile   = round(quantile(reviewer_baselines$reviewer_mean[reviewer_baselines$reviewer_review_count >= min_reviewer_reviews], 0.95), 2)
)

# ---- Restaurant-level comparison ---------------------------------------------

adjusted_summary <- eligible_adjusted_reviews |>
  group_by(business_id) |>
  summarise(
    number_of_reviews_eligible_reviewers = n(),
    average_stars_eligible_reviewers     = mean(stars, na.rm = TRUE),
    average_normalized_score             = mean(normalized_mean_score, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_normalized_score              = median(normalized_mean_score, na.rm = TRUE),
    average_normalized_median_score      = mean(normalized_median_score, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

restaurant_summary <- selected_restaurants |>
  select(business_id, business_name, address, postal_code, latitude, longitude,
         yelp_stars = stars, categories) |>
  left_join(all_reviewer_summary, by = "business_id") |>
  left_join(adjusted_summary, by = "business_id") |>
  arrange(desc(average_normalized_score))

ranked <- restaurant_summary |>
  filter(number_of_reviews_eligible_reviewers >= min_eligible_reviews) |>
  mutate(
    rank_all_reviewers = min_rank(desc(average_stars_all_reviewers)),
    rank_adjusted      = min_rank(desc(average_normalized_score)),
    rank_change        = rank_all_reviewers - rank_adjusted   # positive = moves up
  )

# ---- Top 10 ------------------------------------------------------------------

top10 <- ranked |>
  arrange(desc(average_normalized_score)) |>
  slice_head(n = 10) |>
  mutate(top_rank = row_number())

# Robustness: does the top 10 change with other choices?
top10_with <- function(min_rev, min_elig, score = "average_normalized_score") {
  category_reviews_adjusted |>
    filter(reviewer_review_count >= min_rev) |>
    group_by(business_id) |>
    summarise(n = n(),
              average_normalized_score = mean(normalized_mean_score),
              average_normalized_median_score = mean(normalized_median_score),
              .groups = "drop") |>
    filter(n >= min_elig) |>
    arrange(desc(.data[[score]])) |>
    slice_head(n = 10) |>
    pull(business_id)
}
robustness <- tibble(
  version = c("Reviewers with 3+ reviews", "Reviewers with 10+ reviews",
              "Restaurants need 20+ eligible reviews", "Median baseline instead of mean",
              "Plain average stars (all reviewers)"),
  ids = list(top10_with(3, min_eligible_reviews), top10_with(10, min_eligible_reviews),
             top10_with(min_reviewer_reviews, 20),
             top10_with(min_reviewer_reviews, min_eligible_reviews, "average_normalized_median_score"),
             ranked |> arrange(desc(average_stars_all_reviewers)) |> slice_head(n = 10) |> pull(business_id))
) |>
  mutate(top10_restaurants_kept = sapply(ids, function(x) sum(x %in% top10$business_id))) |>
  select(-ids)

# Biggest movers among ranked restaurants
movers <- bind_rows(
  ranked |> arrange(desc(rank_change)) |> slice_head(n = 5) |> mutate(direction = "up"),
  ranked |> arrange(rank_change) |> slice_head(n = 5) |> mutate(direction = "down")
) |>
  select(direction, business_name, postal_code, number_of_reviews_all_reviewers,
         average_stars_all_reviewers, number_of_reviews_eligible_reviewers,
         average_stars_eligible_reviewers, average_normalized_score,
         rank_all_reviewers, rank_adjusted, rank_change)

# ---- Save --------------------------------------------------------------------

saveRDS(restaurant_summary, "data/new_orleans/restaurant_summary.rds")
write.csv(threshold_table, "data/new_orleans/reviewer_thresholds.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(baseline_check, "data/new_orleans/baseline_check.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(robustness, "data/new_orleans/top10_robustness.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(movers |> mutate(across(where(is.double), ~ round(.x, 2))),
          "data/new_orleans/rank_movers.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(top10 |>
            transmute(top_rank, business_name, address, postal_code,
                      reviews_all = number_of_reviews_all_reviewers,
                      avg_stars_all = round(average_stars_all_reviewers, 2),
                      reviews_eligible = number_of_reviews_eligible_reviewers,
                      avg_stars_eligible = round(average_stars_eligible_reviewers, 2),
                      avg_normalized_score = round(average_normalized_score, 2),
                      rank_all_reviewers),
          "data/new_orleans/top10_restaurants.csv", row.names = FALSE)
saveRDS(top10, "data/new_orleans/top10.rds")
saveRDS(ranked, "data/new_orleans/ranked_restaurants.rds")

print(threshold_table); print(baseline_check); print(robustness)
print(as.data.frame(movers |> mutate(across(where(is.double), ~ round(.x, 2)))))
print(as.data.frame(top10 |> select(top_rank, business_name, postal_code,
                                    number_of_reviews_all_reviewers, average_stars_all_reviewers,
                                    number_of_reviews_eligible_reviewers, average_normalized_score,
                                    rank_all_reviewers)))

# ---- Plot: raw vs. adjusted --------------------------------------------------

mover_names <- c(movers$business_name[movers$direction == "up"][1:2],
                 movers$business_name[movers$direction == "down"][1:2])
plot_data <- ranked |>
  mutate(group = case_when(
    business_id %in% top10$business_id ~ "top10",
    business_name %in% mover_names     ~ "mover",
    TRUE                               ~ "other"
  ))
top_labels   <- plot_data |> filter(group == "top10") |>
  left_join(top10 |> select(business_id, top_rank), by = "business_id")
mover_labels <- plot_data |> filter(group == "mover")

p_adjusted <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(average_stars_all_reviewers, average_normalized_score)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "22", color = theme_cols$ink, linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(data = filter(plot_data, group == "other"), shape = 21, size = 2.6,
             fill = theme_cols$tract[["fill"]], color = "white", stroke = 0.4) +
  geom_point(data = mover_labels, shape = 21, size = 3.6,
             fill = theme_cols$below[["deep"]], color = "white", stroke = 0.8) +
  geom_point(data = top_labels, shape = 21, size = 4.2,
             fill = theme_cols$zcta[["deep"]], color = "white", stroke = 0.8) +
  geom_text_repel(data = top_labels, aes(label = top_rank), family = plot_family,
                  fontface = "bold", color = theme_cols$ink, size = 3.4,
                  min.segment.length = 0.2, segment.color = theme_cols$muted,
                  box.padding = 0.25, point.padding = 0.15, max.overlaps = Inf, seed = 167) +
  geom_label_repel(data = mover_labels,
                   aes(label = paste0(business_name, "\n", rank_all_reviewers, "th \u2192 ", rank_adjusted, "th")),
                   family = plot_family, color = theme_cols$ink, size = 3.2, label.size = 0,
                   fill = alpha("white", 0.85), lineheight = 0.95, min.segment.length = 0,
                   segment.color = theme_cols$muted, box.padding = 0.6, nudge_y = 0.25, seed = 167) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.15, y = 0.85, hjust = 0, label = "rated higher than\nreviewers usually rate",
           family = plot_family, color = theme_cols$muted, size = 3.4, lineheight = 0.9) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.15, y = -1.5, hjust = 0, label = "rated lower than\nreviewers usually rate",
           family = plot_family, color = theme_cols$muted, size = 3.4, lineheight = 0.9) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(1.1, 5), breaks = 1:5) +
  labs(
    title = "Adjusting for reviewer habits mostly agrees with Yelp",
    subtitle = paste0(nrow(ranked), " restaurants with ", min_eligible_reviews,
                      "+ reviews from active reviewers. Orange = top 10, pink = biggest rank changes"),
    x = "average stars from all reviewers",
    y = "average normalized score"
  ) +
  theme_pastel()

save_plot(p_adjusted, "figures/raw_vs_adjusted.png", width = 10, height = 6.6)
message("Saved Step 7 tables in data/new_orleans/ and figures/raw_vs_adjusted.png")

# All maps in the README, plus the ZIP-level reviewer-adjusted summary.

#   figures/new_orleans_boundary_map.png   Step 5: restaurants inside the city
#   figures/zcta_restaurant_count_map.png  Step 6: restaurants per ZIP code

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(dplyr)
  library(sf)
  library(ggplot2)
  library(ggrepel)
})
source("R/theme.R")
sf_use_s2(FALSE)

min_ranked_per_zip <- 10   # ZIPs need this many ranked restaurants to get a score

zcta <- st_read("data/boundaries/zcta_new_orleans.geojson", quiet = TRUE)
nsa  <- st_read("data/boundaries/nsa_new_orleans.geojson", quiet = TRUE)
city <- st_union(nsa) |> st_sf()             # NSAs tile the whole city

selected_restaurants <- readRDS("data/new_orleans/selected_restaurants.rds")
restaurant_areas     <- readRDS("data/new_orleans/restaurant_areas.rds")
ranked               <- readRDS("data/new_orleans/ranked_restaurants.rds") |>
  left_join(restaurant_areas, by = "business_id")
top10                <- readRDS("data/new_orleans/top10.rds") |>
  left_join(restaurant_areas, by = "business_id")

points <- selected_restaurants |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326, remove = FALSE)
points_in_city <- points[lengths(st_within(points, city)) > 0, ]

zcta_city <- st_intersection(zcta, city)     # ZIP shapes clipped to the city
zip_centers <- st_point_on_surface(zcta_city)

map_theme <- theme_pastel() +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), axis.text.x = element_blank(), axis.text.y = element_blank(),
        axis.title = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major = element_blank(), legend.position = "right",
        legend.title = element_text(color = theme_cols$ink, size = 11),
        legend.text = element_text(color = theme_cols$muted))

# ---- ZIP-level reviewer-adjusted summary -------------------------------------

zip_adjusted <- ranked |>
  group_by(zip) |>
  summarise(
    ranked_restaurants       = n(),
    pct_above_usual          = round(100 * mean(average_normalized_score > 0)),
    in_top_10                = sum(business_id %in% top10$business_id),
    in_top_50                = sum(rank_adjusted <= 50),
    average_stars_all        = mean(average_stars_all_reviewers),
    average_normalized_score = mean(average_normalized_score),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(average_normalized_score))
write.csv(zip_adjusted |> mutate(across(c(average_stars_all, average_normalized_score), ~ round(.x, 2))),
          "data/new_orleans/zip_adjusted_scores.csv", row.names = FALSE)
print(as.data.frame(zip_adjusted))

# ---- Map 1: restaurants inside the city boundary (Step 5) --------------------

p_boundary <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = city, fill = "#FBF8F5", color = theme_cols$ink, linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_sf(data = points_in_city |> arrange(stars), aes(fill = stars),
          shape = 21, color = "white", stroke = 0.3, size = 2.4) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#F8D3B3", high = "#9A3F12", limits = c(1, 5),
                      name = "Yelp stars") +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(-90.14, -89.90), ylim = c(29.90, 30.06), expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Breakfast & coffee spots cluster along the river",

save_plot(p_boundary, "figures/new_orleans_boundary_map.png", width = 10, height = 6.6)

zip_counts <- readRDS("data/new_orleans/zcta_summary.rds")
zcta_count_map <- zcta_city |> left_join(zip_counts, by = "area_id")
count_labels <- zip_centers |>
  left_join(zip_counts, by = "area_id") |>
  filter(number_of_restaurants >= 10)

p_zcta <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = zcta_count_map, aes(fill = number_of_restaurants), color = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_sf(data = city, fill = NA, color = theme_cols$ink, linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_sf_text(data = count_labels, aes(label = paste0(area_id, "\n", number_of_restaurants)),
               family = plot_family, size = 3, color = theme_cols$ink, lineheight = 0.9,
               fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#FFF1E5", high = "#D9844F", na.value = "#F4F1EE",
                      name = "Breakfast &\ncoffee spots") +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(-90.14, -89.90), ylim = c(29.90, 30.06), expand = FALSE) +

save_plot(p_zcta, "figures/zcta_restaurant_count_map.png", width = 10, height = 6.6)

# ---- Map 3: the answer - top 10 and ZIP-level adjusted scores ----------------

zip_score_map <- zcta_city |>
  left_join(zip_adjusted, by = c("area_id" = "zip")) |>
  mutate(score = ifelse(ranked_restaurants >= min_ranked_per_zip, average_normalized_score, NA))

score_labels <- zip_centers |>
  left_join(zip_adjusted, by = c("area_id" = "zip")) |>
  filter(ranked_restaurants >= min_ranked_per_zip)

top10_points <- top10 |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326, remove = FALSE)

view <- list(x = c(-90.135, -90.02), y = c(29.915, 30.03))

p_top10 <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = zip_score_map, aes(fill = score), color = "white", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_sf(data = city, fill = NA, color = theme_cols$ink, linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_sf(data = points_in_city, shape = 16, size = 0.9, color = alpha(theme_cols$ink, 0.25)) +
  geom_sf_text(data = score_labels, aes(label = area_id), family = plot_family,
               size = 3, color = alpha(theme_cols$ink, 0.55), fontface = "bold",
               nudge_y = -0.004) +
  geom_sf(data = top10_points, shape = 21, size = 6.5, fill = theme_cols$zcta[["deep"]],
          color = "white", stroke = 1.1) +
  geom_sf_text(data = top10_points, aes(label = top_rank), family = plot_family,
               size = 3.1, color = "white", fontface = "bold") +
  geom_label_repel(data = top10, aes(longitude, latitude, label = business_name),
                   family = plot_family, size = 3.2, color = theme_cols$ink,

                   box.padding = 0.7, point.padding = 0.6, min.segment.length = 0,
                   segment.color = theme_cols$muted, max.overlaps = Inf, seed = 10) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = theme_cols$below[["deep"]], mid = "#F2EEEA",
                       high = theme_cols$above[["deep"]], midpoint = 0,
                       limits = c(-0.25, 0.25), oob = scales::squish, na.value = "#FAF8F6",
                       name = "ZIP average\nnormalized score",

8 How sure is the top 10?

Changing one choice at a time:

Version Restaurants still in the top 10
Reviewers with 3+ reviews count as active 6 of 10
Reviewers with 10+ reviews count as active 6 of 10
Median baseline instead of mean 8 of 10
Restaurants need 20+ active-reviewer reviews 3 of 10
Plain Yelp average (no adjustment) 5 of 10

The exact list is sensitive, mostly because many top restaurants are small, with 10 to 20 active-reviewer reviews. The area answer is steadier: in every adjusted version, Mid-City (70119) and Bywater & Marigny (70117) together hold at least half of the top 10.

9 Limitations

  • The data stops in January 2022. Some restaurants may have closed or changed since then.
  • Yelp categories are broad. “Cafes” and “Coffee & Tea” also tag gelato shops (Angelo Brocato) and sandwich counters (Shank Charcuterie), so a few top-10 spots are not classic breakfast places.
  • Active reviewers are a small group. The adjusted score rests on 3.5% of reviewers, whose tastes may differ from a typical visitor’s.
  • Small samples. Restaurants need only 10 active-reviewer reviews to be ranked, so the exact order could change with more data.
  • ZIP codes are not neighbourhoods. A ZIP code average mixes very different streets.

10 Conclusion

For breakfast and coffee in New Orleans, the best area is just outside downtown. Bywater & St. Roch (70117) has the highest ratings on both measures, and Mid-City (70119) holds the most top-10 spots. Downtown 70130 has the most options, but its restaurants are, on average, rated slightly below what their reviewers usually give.

Adjusting for reviewer habits mostly confirms Yelp’s ratings, but it lifts a few places loved by active reviewers (First Cup Cafe) and drops a few that only casual reviewers rate highly.

A high star average from hundreds of easy reviewers is weaker evidence than a good score from people who are hard to impress.

![](figures/top10_map.png){fig-alt="Map of the top 10 breakfast and coffee restaurants in New Orleans, with ZIP codes coloured by reviewer-adjusted score"}

## The question

New Orleans is famous for its breakfasts: beignets, brunch and chicory coffee. But with one morning to spare, **where should you go?**

> **Where can someone find the best breakfast and coffee in New Orleans, and which area of the city is best for finding it?**

A plain star average has two problems. Some restaurants have only a handful of reviews, and some reviewers give everything five stars while others almost never do. So in this project, “best” means:

1. **Rated well by reviewers who are hard to impress.** Each review is compared with that reviewer’s own usual rating (the *adjusted score*).
2. **Enough evidence.** A restaurant needs at least 10 reviews from active reviewers to be ranked.
3. **For areas:** lots of good options, and restaurants that are rated above reviewers’ usual more often than not.

## The data, and how the huge files were handled

The project uses two files from the [Yelp Open Dataset](https://business.yelp.com/data/resources/open-dataset/): the **business file** (113 MB, 150,346 businesses) and the **review file** (**5.1 GB, 6,990,280 reviews**, from 2005 to January 2022).

::: {.plain}
The review file is bigger than a laptop’s memory can comfortably hold. So instead of opening it all at once, the code reads it **100,000 reviews at a time**, keeps only the reviews of New Orleans restaurants, and throws the rest away before reading the next batch.
:::

- **Streaming import.** Both files are read with `jsonlite::stream_in()` and a handler function. Each batch is cut down to the needed columns before the next is read. Scanning all 7 million reviews took about **6 minutes**.
- **Only what’s needed.** Only the business and review files are pulled out of the Yelp archive.
- **Small, compressed outputs.** Results are saved as `xz`-compressed `.rds` files. Review text is stored separately: the review table without text is 15 MB, the text alone 71 MB.
- **Raw files stay local.** The raw JSON files are several gigabytes, more than GitHub allows, so they are listed in `.gitignore` and can be deleted once the `.rds` files are saved.

## Choosing the restaurants

**New Orleans restaurants.** A business counts if `state` is `LA`, its `city` is “New Orleans”, and its categories include “Restaurants”. That gives **2,261 restaurants**.

**Breakfast & coffee.** Four categories describe places you’d go for a morning meal or a coffee break: *Breakfast & Brunch*, *Coffee & Tea*, *Cafes* and *Bakeries*.

![](figures/category_chart.png){fig-alt="Bar chart of the most common restaurant categories, with the four breakfast and coffee categories highlighted"}

These four belong together because they often appear on the **same** restaurant:

| Category pair | Restaurants with both |
|:---|---:|
| Breakfast & Brunch + Coffee & Tea | 85 |
| Cafes + Coffee & Tea | 75 |
| Breakfast & Brunch + Cafes | 65 |
| Bakeries + Coffee & Tea | 37 |
| Bakeries + Breakfast & Brunch | 32 |
| Bakeries + Cafes | 16 |

::: {.plain}
A restaurant is included if it has **at least one** of the four categories. That gives **575 restaurants** spread over 24 ZIP code areas, far more than the required 10 restaurants in 7 areas. Their **159,552 reviews**, from 97,950 different reviewers, were pulled out before any further analysis.
:::

## Checking the city boundary

Yelp’s `city` field is just text typed by the business. To check it, each restaurant’s latitude and longitude were matched to the official city boundary from the U.S. Census with a spatial join.

| Yelp city | Official place | Restaurants |
|:---|:---|---:|
| New Orleans | New Orleans | 564 |
| New Orleans | Elmwood | 2 |
| New Orleans | Harahan | 2 |
| New Orleans | Jefferson | 2 |
| New Orleans | Metairie | 2 |
| New Orleans | Terrytown | 2 |
| New Orleans | Kenner | 1 |

::: {.plain}
11 restaurants have a New Orleans mailing address but sit just outside the city limits, in Jefferson Parish. They are real nearby options, so they stay in.
:::

![](figures/new_orleans_boundary_map.png){fig-alt="Map of breakfast and coffee restaurants inside the New Orleans city boundary, coloured by Yelp stars"}

## Choosing a way to divide the city

To compare areas, the city has to be divided up somehow. Three systems were tested:

- **ZIP Code Tabulation Areas**, the Census version of ZIP codes;
- **Neighborhood Statistical Areas**, the City of New Orleans’ own planning neighbourhoods;
- **Census tracts**, statistical areas built for population data.

| System | Areas with a restaurant | Assigned | Unmatched | Smallest | Largest | Median per area | Areas with < 5 |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| ZIP codes | 24 | 575 | 0 | 1 | 143 | 6.5 | 9 (38%) |
| Neighbourhoods | 54 | 564 | 11 | 1 | 119 | 4 | 28 (52%) |
| Census tracts | 103 | 564 | 11 | 1 | 117 | 2 | 75 (73%) |

![](figures/geographic_system_comparison.png){fig-alt="Scatter plots of restaurants per area against average rating for ZIP codes, neighbourhoods and census tracts"}

::: {.plain}
The smaller the areas, the fewer restaurants each one holds, and the more one restaurant can swing the average. Three out of four census tracts have fewer than 5 breakfast spots.
:::

::: {.decision}
**The choice: ZIP codes**

enough restaurants per area · easy to understand · every restaurant matched
:::

- **Enough restaurants to compare.** ZIP codes pool enough restaurants for the averages to mean something.
- **Easy to understand.** Anyone knows a ZIP code. Few people know their census tract number.
- **Nothing left out.** Every restaurant was matched to a ZIP code, including the 11 just outside the city.

**What ZIP codes hide.** ZIP codes are postal areas, not neighbourhoods. 70130 alone covers the Warehouse District and part of the French Quarter, so a great café and a tourist trap share one average. The 9 ZIP codes with fewer than 5 breakfast spots are mapped but not ranked.

![](figures/zcta_restaurant_count_map.png){fig-alt="Map of the number of breakfast and coffee restaurants in each ZIP code"}

![](figures/zip_ratings_chart.png){fig-alt="Average Yelp stars by ZIP code compared with the city average"}

## Adjusting for reviewer habits

Some reviewers give almost every restaurant five stars; others rarely do. A 4-star review means more from a tough reviewer than from an easy one.

::: {.plain}
For each reviewer, work out their **usual rating**. Then score every review as *stars given minus that reviewer’s usual*. A reviewer who usually gives 3 stars and gives a place 4 adds **+1**. A reviewer who usually gives 5 and gives 4 adds **−1**. A restaurant’s adjusted score is the average of these.
:::

**Who counts as an active reviewer?** A usual rating only means something if the reviewer has rated enough places. Reviewers with at least **5 breakfast & coffee reviews** were kept:

| Minimum reviews | Reviewers kept | Share of reviewers | Reviews kept | Share of reviews | Restaurants ranked |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 3 | 11,531 | 11.8% | 57,617 | 36.1% | 448 |
| **5** | **3,416** | **3.5%** | **30,918** | **19.4%** | **394** |
| 10 | 784 | 0.8% | 14,919 | 9.4% | 325 |

Only 3.5% of reviewers qualify, but they wrote almost a fifth of all reviews. A higher threshold gives each reviewer a better baseline, but leaves fewer restaurants to rank.

**Mean or median?** The **mean** was used as each reviewer’s usual rating. Ratings are whole stars, so with a median baseline **49%** of reviews get an adjusted score of exactly 0, throwing away most of the information. With the mean, only 5% do. The typical active reviewer averages 4.0 stars, but the range is wide: 2.9 at the 5th percentile, 4.8 at the 95th.

![](figures/raw_vs_adjusted.png){fig-alt="Scatter plot of plain Yelp averages against reviewer-adjusted scores, with the top 10 and the biggest rank changes highlighted"}

Ranks before and after adjustment are strongly related (rank correlation **0.83**), but a few restaurants move hundreds of places:

| Restaurant | ZIP | Stars (all reviewers) | Stars (active reviewers) | Rank before | Rank after |
|:---|:---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| First Cup Cafe | 70125 | 3.44 | 4.47 | 331st | **12th** |

The moves have two causes. **Reviewer behaviour:** First Cup Cafe’s active reviewers rate it a full star higher than casual reviewers do. **Small samples:** most of these restaurants have only 10 to 25 active-reviewer reviews, so a few reviews move them a long way.

## How sure is the top 10?

Changing one choice at a time:

| Version | Restaurants still in the top 10 |
|:---|---:|
| Reviewers with 3+ reviews count as active | 6 of 10 |
| Reviewers with 10+ reviews count as active | 6 of 10 |
| Median baseline instead of mean | 8 of 10 |
| Restaurants need 20+ active-reviewer reviews | 3 of 10 |
| Plain Yelp average (no adjustment) | 5 of 10 |

::: {.plain}
The exact list is sensitive, mostly because many top restaurants are small, with 10 to 20 active-reviewer reviews. The **area** answer is steadier: in every adjusted version, Mid-City (70119) and Bywater & Marigny (70117) together hold at least half of the top 10.
:::

## Limitations

- **The data stops in January 2022.** Some restaurants may have closed or changed since then.
- **Yelp categories are broad.** “Cafes” and “Coffee & Tea” also tag gelato shops (Angelo Brocato) and sandwich counters (Shank Charcuterie), so a few top-10 spots are not classic breakfast places.
- **Active reviewers are a small group.** The adjusted score rests on 3.5% of reviewers, whose tastes may differ from a typical visitor’s.
- **Small samples.** Restaurants need only 10 active-reviewer reviews to be ranked, so the exact order could change with more data.
- **ZIP codes are not neighbourhoods.** A ZIP code average mixes very different streets.

## Conclusion

For breakfast and coffee in New Orleans, the best area is **just outside downtown**. Bywater & St. Roch (70117) has the highest ratings on both measures, and Mid-City (70119) holds the most top-10 spots. Downtown 70130 has the most options, but its restaurants are, on average, rated slightly below what their reviewers usually give.

Adjusting for reviewer habits mostly confirms Yelp’s ratings, but it lifts a few places loved by active reviewers (First Cup Cafe) and drops a few that only casual reviewers rate highly.

::: {.plain}
A high star average from hundreds of easy reviewers is weaker evidence than a good score from people who are hard to impress.
:::
